title: Professional evaluation: Realistic tasks complicate reproducible scoring
desc: Tests execution rather than answers, with automated judging and self-correction requiring their own validation.

kps.k: The central proposition is that credible AI evaluation must test professional task execution, not just the quality of isolated answers.
kps.d: JADE argues that objectively scored search, coding and reasoning tasks offer reproducibility but cover only part of professional work. A Survey on Evaluation of LLM-based Agents adds that agents must make sequential decisions, use tools and interact with changing environments. TheAgentCompany calls for tasks grounded in multiple occupational categories before drawing conclusions about work automation. Together, these arguments distinguish benchmark success from demonstrated readiness for a workplace role.

qs.q: Most existing agent benchmarks focus on tasks with verifiable outcomes, such as multi-hop web search (Wei et al., 2025; Zhou et al., 2025b; Chen et al., 2025b), code generation (Jimenez et al., 2024; Quan et al., 2025), or toolmediated reasoning (Yao et al., 2025a; Wang et al., 2026; Barres et al., 2025), enabling objective and reproducible evaluation.
qs.a: JADE: Expert-Grounded Dynamic Evaluation for Open-Ended Professional Tasks · Academia · 2026

qs.q: Such evaluation must go beyond measuring LLM textual outputs to assess an agent’s capacity for sequential decision-making and operation within dynamic environments.
qs.a: A Survey on Evaluation of LLM-based Agents · Academia · 2025

kps.k: Open-ended professional work creates a tension between reproducible scoring and context-sensitive judgment.
kps.d: JADE argues that strategic analysis and evidence synthesis admit multiple valid responses, so assessment needs consistent professional principles and current evidence checks rather than a single reference answer. Its supplier-search example illustrates the argument; the supplied excerpt does not report a validated method or specify who performs the checks. RubricEval supplies a narrower qualification: it studies binary rubric judgments, excludes comparative and Likert-scale ratings, and acknowledges that some difficult cases may be missing. These passages establish different evaluation scopes, not evidence that one scoring format outperforms another.

qs.q: These tasks rarely admit a single “gold” answer, making realistic evaluation an unresolved challenge.
qs.a: JADE: Expert-Grounded Dynamic Evaluation for Open-Ended Professional Tasks · Academia · 2026

kps.k: Reported task-level results show useful autonomy alongside substantial limits, without measuring job replacement.
kps.d: The supplied September 2025 version of TheAgentCompany reports that Gemini 2.5 Pro completed 30.3% of tasks autonomously and scored 39.3% with partial credit; all tested models used OpenHands. The authors distinguish these capabilities from comprehensive automation even within well-scoped software-company administrative and coding tasks. Separately, the agent-evaluation survey reports planning difficulties, persistent-memory weaknesses and performance below 25% Pass@1 on SWE-bench Pro. Those survey figures come from cited benchmarks, not new experiments, and the different metrics and task sets do not support direct comparisons.

qs.q: We find in experiments that the best performing model, Gemini 2.5 Pro was able to autonomously perform 30.3% of the provided tests to completion, and achieve a score of 39.3% on our metric that provides extra credit for partially completed tasks.
qs.a: TheAgentCompany: Benchmarking LLM Agents on Consequential Real World Tasks · Academia · 2024

qs.q: Model performance remains below 25% Pass@1, highlighting current limitations in handling long-horizon, complex code changes.

kps.k: Realistic tasks do not by themselves guarantee valid or reproducible measurements.
kps.d: The agent-evaluation survey reports Xue and colleagues’ criticism of overly optimistic WebVoyager estimates. It also describes follow-up criticism of SWE-bench’s tests, issue descriptions and execution environments, despite its grounding in real GitHub issues. Human filtering, containerised execution and difficulty annotations in SWE-bench Verified seek to address these defects. The practical implication is to examine task specification, scoring and execution conditions alongside headline performance, while updating benchmarks as capabilities and deployment settings change.

qs.q: Several follow-up works identified evaluation issues, like overly specific or unrelated unit tests, underspecified issue descriptions, and problematic environmental setups, and thus proposed new variants (SWE-bench Lite, 2024; Xia et al., 2024; OpenAI, 2024; Aleithan et al., 2024).
qs.a: A Survey on Evaluation of LLM-based Agents · Academia · 2025

kps.k: Automated judging and self-correction remain evaluation tools whose reliability requires separate assessment.
kps.d: Agent-as-a-Judge’s related-work discussion reports applications of LLM judging to dialogue, multimodal feedback and code validation, including qualitative claims that ICE-Score better aligns with human preferences and functional correctness. It supplies no results for its own method. The agent-evaluation survey cautions that measuring self-reflection only through final-answer improvement gives a coarse, prompt-dependent measure and identifies a continuing standardisation gap. These are complementary accounts of potential and measurement limits, not a demonstrated head-to-head disagreement. Neither establishes that automated assessment can replace expert judgment or human verification before reliance.

qs.q: LLM-as-a-Judge In the domain of AI evaluation and judgment, frameworks (Zheng et al., 2024; Fu et al., 2023) have pioneered the use of LLMs to assess conversational agents, demonstrating how LLMs can evaluate dialogue quality and consistency.
qs.a: Agent-as-a-Judge: Evaluate Agents with Agents · Academia · 2024

qs.q: Improvement was typically measured by determining if the final answer was corrected, providing only a coarse evaluation and potentially ill-defined measurement, as observed improvements may depend on specific prompting techniques lacking proper standardization (Huang et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2025).
qs.a: A Survey on Evaluation of LLM-based Agents · Academia · 2025

kps.k: The supplied evidence supports a measurement agenda more strongly than conclusions about legal reliability, productivity or economic displacement.
kps.d: The agent-evaluation survey prioritises cost-efficiency, safety, robustness and fine-grained scalable assessment, but provides no quantified findings on those dimensions here. Most other supplied material consists of bibliographies or disclosures: GDPval, the experienced-developer productivity study, LegalBench and the legal-hallucination studies supply no substantive results in these excerpts. References to evaluator bias, human–AI collaboration or conflicting productivity claims therefore identify research questions rather than resolve them. Practical conclusions should remain tied to the tested task, system configuration and scoring method; these excerpts cannot establish legal error rates, workplace productivity effects or the adequacy of human oversight.

qs.q: We also identify critical gaps that future research must address—particularly in assessing cost-efficiency, safety, and robustness, and in developing fine-grained, scalable evaluation methods 1.
qs.a: A Survey on Evaluation of LLM-based Agents · Academia · 2025

vlens.an: The curated legal-tech-vendor sources cannot be assigned a substantive collective position on the proposition. Most supplied excerpts are bibliographies rather than the sources’ own methods, findings or arguments, so citations to realistic agent tasks, evaluator bias, human-in-the-loop standards and judge benchmarks cannot be treated as endorsements. PRBench provides the clearest source-authored indication of relevance by exploring model performance with web-search and code-interpreter access, which concerns tool-enabled execution rather than isolated answers; however, the excerpt reports no procedure or results and says nothing about reproducibility or scoring validity. Xpertbench, GDPval and LeMAJ cite work on expert tasks and automated judges, but their own views on whether those judges require separate validation remain undetermined. Other excerpts are either entirely bibliographic or do not materially address the proposition. Thus there is thematic alignment with the cluster’s measurement agenda, but insufficient attributable evidence to conclude that this professional voice supports, extends or rejects it; this assessment applies only to the curated sources, not legal-tech vendors generally.

qs.q: Evaluations with Web Search & Code Interpreter In this section, we explore the performance of chat models when given access to web search and code interpreter tools.
qs.a: PRBench: Large-Scale Expert Rubrics for Evaluating High-Stakes Professional Reasoning · Legal-tech vendor · 2025

vlens.an: The supplied excerpts do not establish a substantive position attributable to this professional voice. They consist entirely of bibliography entries or fragments, so citation of relevant work cannot be treated as endorsement of the cluster’s proposition. The references nevertheless show thematic overlap: the NIST excerpt points to real-world agent tasks and evaluation frameworks; the statistical-evaluation bibliography covers uncertainty, nondeterminism, benchmark defects and measurement validity; and the interdisciplinary-review bibliography includes concerns about whether benchmarks reflect professional needs and support reproducible evaluation. LexRubric supplies no substantive evidence at all. This variation indicates several potentially relevant emphases—task realism, statistical reliability, validity and sociotechnical relevance—but no source-level findings or reasoning from which to infer acceptance, extension or rejection of the proposition that professional evaluation must test task execution and separately validate scoring, automated judging and self-correction. Because these are curated sources, this evidentiary limitation should not be generalized to regulators, courts or professional bodies as a whole.

qs.q: Benchmark datasets driving artificial   intelligence development fail to capture the needs of medical professionals.
qs.a: Can We Trust AI Benchmarks? An Interdisciplinary Review of Current Issues in AI Evaluation · Regulators & courts · 2025

vlens.an: The substantive academia-and-research sources accept the proposition’s core and materially develop it into a broader measurement agenda. Their common rationale is that credible evaluation must observe sequential decisions, tool use, environmental interaction and occupationally grounded task completion—not infer workplace readiness from isolated answers or narrow proxy tasks. They add concrete design requirements: varied real-world job categories, partial-credit checkpoints, reproducible execution environments, expert-grounded principles for open-ended work, current evidence checks, and separate validation of automated judges and self-correction measures. Material variation concerns scope and evidentiary strength rather than overall direction. TheAgentCompany supplies empirical task-level results and cautions that partial autonomy does not demonstrate job replacement; the agent-evaluation survey synthesises benchmark design, capability limits and standardisation gaps; JADE conceptually addresses professional tasks with multiple valid answers; and RubricEval narrowly highlights the bounded coverage of binary rubric judgments. Agent-as-a-Judge discusses possible automated-evaluation methods but does not establish their independent validity. Most other supplied records are bibliography-only or disclosures, so their positions are genuinely unclear and cannot be treated as corroborating the proposition. Because this is a curated corpus, this synthesis describes the relationship among the supplied sources, not the prevalence of these views across academia and research generally.

qs.q: Such evaluation must go beyond measuring LLM textual outputs to assess an agent’s capacity for sequential decision-making and operation within dynamic environments.

qs.q: For example, a query for “FDA-certified suppliers for stainless steel tumblers with low shipping cost to the USA” admits multiple valid response strategies, whose quality cannot be reliably assessed without consistent professional principles and real-time evidence verification.
qs.a: JADE: Expert-Grounded Dynamic Evaluation for Open-Ended Professional Tasks · Academia · 2026

elens.an: The only supplied source-level record for the 2015–2022 period contains bibliographic references rather than substantive claims, evidence, predictions, or recommendations. Although the cited topics include benchmarks and error reporting, citation alone does not show whether the source accepts the proposition that credible evaluation must test realistic professional task execution or that automated scoring and self-correction require separate validation. There is therefore no basis for identifying support, opposition, or a constructive alternative, and no broader inference should be drawn from this curated single-source record.

The usable substantive evidence from this period builds on the proposition that credible evaluation should test realistic professional task execution rather than isolated answers. TheAgentCompany concretely extends that agenda by requiring occupationally grounded tasks across multiple job categories, evaluating long-horizon work with checkpoints and partial credit, and distinguishing measured task completion from comprehensive workplace automation. Material internal variation is primarily evidentiary rather than argumentative: Agent-as-a-Judge discusses tool-using agents, automated judging and continuing hallucination or coherence problems, but the supplied excerpts do not establish its own validation results; nearly all other records are bibliography-only and therefore have no determinable position. Those bibliographies identify related concerns—reproducibility, benchmark sensitivity, evaluator bias and limits of self-correction—but citation alone cannot show endorsement. No supplied substantive source rejects the proposition, but the curated selection and the large amount of indeterminate material preclude treating this position as representative of the period or as evidence of prevalence.

elens.an: The usable 2025 evidence builds materially on the proposition. A Survey on Evaluation of LLM-based Agents agrees that credible evaluation must move beyond isolated text outputs to sequential, tool-mediated action in dynamic environments. It extends the proposition by specifying relevant dimensions—including planning, state tracking, tool use, memory and error recovery—and by showing that greater task realism does not itself ensure valid measurement: benchmark specifications, tests and execution environments can produce misleading or irreproducible results. It also directly reinforces the need to validate self-correction separately, because apparent improvement can be prompt-dependent and measured only coarsely. Material variation concerns evidentiary strength rather than substantive disagreement: most other supplied 2025 excerpts are bibliographies or fragments that identify adjacent topics such as evaluator bias, reproducibility, professional benchmarks and verification, but do not establish their sources’ own positions. They therefore remain unclear and should not be treated as corroboration or opposition. Because this is a curated selection, this assessment characterises only the supplied evidence and does not imply prevalence across 2025 sources generally.

elens.an: The substantively usable 2026 evidence supports the cluster proposition, while most supplied records are too fragmentary to classify. JADE directly argues that objectively reproducible proxy benchmarks capture only a limited share of real professional deployment and that open-ended work permits multiple valid approaches, requiring professional principles and current evidence verification. RubricEval supports the narrower measurement claim by restricting itself to binary rubric-level judgments and acknowledging that genuinely difficult cases may be excluded, reinforcing that automated scoring formats need validation and have bounded coverage. Material variation lies in scope: JADE addresses realistic professional task execution and the resulting reproducibility–judgment tension; RubricEval addresses the limitations of one judging format without testing professional workflows. The remaining sources largely consist only of bibliographies, disclosures or fragments. Their references touch on realistic tasks, nondeterminism, benchmark validity, automated judges, verification and self-correction, but citation alone cannot establish those sources’ own positions. Thus the period-level classification rests on the limited substantive evidence and should not be read as representative of all 2026 sources or as evidence of prevalence.
